name: Coppertone sunscreen
lead: Coppertone is a U.S. sun care brand of sunscreens and suntan lotions. People use sunscreen products like it for appearance in two ways: to keep skin looking even and youthful by limiting UV exposure, which Wikipedia's sunscreen article links to smoother skin over time, and to tan with less burning, the use the brand was built around [1][3].

According to Wikipedia, Coppertone traces to a suntan lotion developed by pharmacist Benjamin Green in 1944 and is described as the leading U.S. sun care brand. Its early marketing centred on tanning, with the slogan 'Tan, don't burn' [1]. Its best-known imagery is the 'Little Miss Coppertone' ad, in which a puppy tugs at a girl's swimsuit to reveal a tan line [1].

Evidence on photoaging and sunscreens comes from studies of sunscreens in general rather than this brand: a 2013 Australian study of about 900 white participants found that people assigned daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years had smoother, more resilient skin than controls, and a small study of 32 people reported reversal of photoaging within 12 weeks of daily SPF 30 use [3]. Few clinical studies concern Coppertone specifically.

paras: Green developed the lotion in 1944 to deepen tans. The original logo was a profile of an American Indian chief; in 1953 a Florida agency, Tally Embry Advertising, created the girl-and-puppy concept, and artist Joyce Ballantyne Brand redrew it in 1959 after a fire destroyed the original [1]. A mechanical Coppertone sign still stands in Miami Beach [1].

Plough acquired the brand in 1957; it passed to Schering-Plough in 1971, Merck in 2009 and Bayer in 2014, and in 2019 Beiersdorf announced it would acquire it [1]. Wikipedia also says a product originally made for the U.S. military was adapted for Coppertone in the early 1950s [3].

Wikipedia's sunscreen article places Green's 1944 product in context: he produced 'Red Vet Pet' for US troops in the Pacific during the Second World War, and Coppertone and Bain de Soleil commercialised similar products in the early 1950s. Earlier milestones include L'Oreal's first sunscreen in 1936 and Franz Greiter's 1946 Gletscher Creme, which became the basis for Piz Buin, and water-resistant sunscreens arrived in 1977 [3].
The line now consists mostly of sunscreens plus other skin care, and many products share a distinctive fragrance [1].

Critic Chandler Burr called the shared fragrance 'arguably the single greatest work of scent branding ever', as quoted by Wikipedia [1]. Mechanical Little Miss Coppertone billboards once showed the dog and swimsuit rocking; one still stands in Miami Beach [1].

Wikipedia's sunscreen article describes mineral filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) and chemical filters that absorb UV and release it as heat, with hybrids combining both. UVB causes most sunburn and SPF measures the fraction of burning UV reaching the skin; SPF 15 lets about one-fifteenth through when 2 mg/cm2 is applied. UVA penetrates deeper, contributes to DNA damage and melanoma risk, and broad-spectrum products cover both [3].

The sunscreen article notes that most people apply less than the tested amount, roughly 35 ml for an adult body or a quarter to a third of a teaspoon for the face in the FDA test, which can make the effective SPF lower than the label; it describes guidance of SPF 30 or higher with reapplication, especially after water [3].

In the US, sunscreen is regulated as an over-the-counter drug rather than a cosmetic. The 2011 rules defined broad spectrum and banned 'sunblock' and 'waterproof' claims; as of 2021 only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were classed as generally recognised as safe and effective, and in 2021 an independent lab found benzene contamination in 27 percent of aerosol sunscreens tested, leading to voluntary recalls across brands [3]. The article also lists allergic contact dermatitis from some filters, reduced vitamin D synthesis with sunscreen use, and environmental concern about oxybenzone and octinoxate on coral [3].

No studies found that evaluate Coppertone sunscreens' effects on skin cancer or sunburn in people. Related laboratory work includes a 1981 hairless-mouse study comparing protective factors across seven sunscreens [2], and a 2021 laboratory study that used Coppertone lotion as a base for botanical mosquito repellents, which concerned repellency rather than sun protection [4].

card.summary: Classic U.S. sunscreen and suntan-lotion brand famous for its pigtailed-girl ad; brand-specific clinical evidence is essentially absent.
card.note: Evidence concerns sunscreens generally, not this brand.

quick.overview:
Coppertone is a U.S. sun care brand that began as a 1944 suntan lotion and became known for its girl-and-puppy advertising.
It is now mostly a sunscreen line, owned by Beiersdorf after a 2019 announced acquisition from Bayer.
quick.mechanism: As a sunscreen brand it relies on UV filters.
quick.risks: No brand-specific clinical safety studies were found. Early marketing emphasised tanning, and its history reflects changing sun-care norms.

chain: Sunscreen filters UV before it reaches the skin
Smoother, more even skin over years; tan builds with less burning
angle.text: Coppertone products are applied before sun exposure. Users apply them to reduce burning and photoaging while tanning or spending time outdoors.
